content.question_text: What is a sealed class in Java?

core_requirements: A class that controls which classes may inherit from it.
It restricts the direct subclasses to a specific list.
acceptable_variations: A class that limits which classes can extend it.
A class with a fixed set of permitted subclasses.

content.question_text: Declare an example sealed class with its permitted subclasses.

core_requirements: Syntax: public abstract sealed class ClassName permits Subclass1, Subclass2 { }
Example: public abstract sealed class JSONValue permits JSONArray, JSONNumber, JSONString { }
acceptable_variations: sealed class Shape permits Circle, Rectangle { }
public sealed class Node permits Element, Text { }

content.question_text: What is required from permitted subclasses when it comes to accessibility?

core_requirements: Permitted subclasses must be accessible.
They cannot be private classes that are nested inside another class (unless nested in the sealed class itself).
They cannot be package-visible classes from another package.
acceptable_variations: They must be accessible to the sealed class.
Private nested classes in other classes are not allowed.

content.question_text: What is required from permitted subclasses that are public?

core_requirements: Public permitted subclasses must be in the same package as the sealed class.
They must be accessible.
acceptable_variations: They must be in the same package.

content.question_text: How does the rule for public permitted subclasses change when you use modules?

core_requirements: They only need to be in the same module (not necessarily the same package).
acceptable_variations: Same module is sufficient.
They can be in different packages within the same module.

content.question_text: Can a sealed class be declared without a permits clause? What happens then?

core_requirements: Yes, a sealed class can be declared without a permits clause.
Then all of its direct subclasses must be declared in the same file.
Programmers without access to that file cannot form subclasses.
acceptable_variations: Yes, all permitted subclasses must be in the same file.

content.question_text: What benefit is connected to sealed classes and pattern matching with switch expressions?

core_requirements: The compiler can check that all direct subclasses are covered as cases.
No default clause is needed if all permitted subclasses are listed.
acceptable_variations: Exhaustiveness checking — the compiler knows all possible subclasses.
No default case required when all subclasses are handled.

content.question_text: Does a permitted subclass of a sealed class need to be final?

core_requirements: No.
Permitted subclasses can be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
acceptable_variations: No, they have three options.

content.question_text: Can a permitted subclass of a sealed class also be sealed?

core_requirements: Yes.
acceptable_variations: Yes, it can be sealed.
Yes, it can further restrict its own subclasses.

content.question_text: What must a subclass of a sealed class specify regarding its inheritance control?

core_requirements: It must specify whether it is sealed.
It must specify whether it is final.
It must specify whether it is non-sealed (open for subclassing).
acceptable_variations: Must be declared as final, sealed, or non-sealed.

content.question_text: What does it mean when a permitted subclass is declared as non-sealed?

core_requirements: It means the class is open for subclassing.
Any class can extend it, regardless of the sealed hierarchy.
acceptable_variations: It allows unlimited subclassing.
It reopens the class for extension.

content.question_text: What is special about the non-sealed keyword?

core_requirements: It is the first Java keyword with a hyphen.
It is a contextual keyword — you can still use 'sealed' as a variable or method name.
There is no ambiguity with subtraction (non - sealed).
acceptable_variations: First hyphenated keyword in Java.
Contextual keyword, not a reserved word.
